title: Trade, rights and development: where UK policy succeeds and falls short
label: 20 October 2026 · Trade in a turbulent world
summary: Witnesses from the TUC, Trade Justice Movement and Institute of Development Studies told the committee that the UK has improved the rhetoric on labour, environment and development in trade policy, but delivery is patchy. They praised some UK actions—such as labour commitments with the EU, market access changes and the Trade Advocacy Fund—while flagging weak enforcement in agreements with countries that restrict workers’ rights, the democratic gap around newer non-binding deals, and the risks posed by investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS). They urged more funded practical support for developing countries’ productive capacity, clearer parliamentary scrutiny, and removing ISDS from future deals.

glossary.definition: World Trade Organization, the multilateral body that sets international trade rules and runs dispute processes.
Developing Countries Trading Scheme, the UK’s unilateral tariff preference system launched in 2023.
Economic Partnership Agreements, trade deals the EU made with some developing regions to replace colonial-era arrangements.
Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, a multilateral Pacific trade pact the UK joined.
Investor‑State Dispute Settlement, a legal route allowing foreign investors to sue states before international tribunals.
African Continental Free Trade Area, a continent-wide trade agreement among African countries.
A UK fund that pays for negotiation support and capacity building for developing countries in trade talks.
Gulf migrant-worker sponsorship system limiting workers' rights and employment mobility.

chapters.title: Where UK trade policy meets labour rights
chapters.takeaway: The UK has made stronger labour commitments in some agreements and improved engagement with unions, but enforcement is inconsistent.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’ll start by asking witnesses for their assessment of UK trade policy on labour, development and environment—what's working and what isn't?

turns.speaker: Lord McDonald of Salford
turns.text: Please talk about strengths and weaknesses across those three areas. Rosa, first to you on labour.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: The trade strategy promised 'strong labour provisions' and we welcome that—especially the UK‑EU 'level playing field' pledge to not regress from 2020 standards, which includes a sanctions route.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: The UK‑Switzerland deal also made labour provisions subject to dispute settlement—useful precedents. The Government now engage more with unions through forums and advisory groups.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: But the UK has signed or pursued deals with countries where independent unions are banned—Vietnam, some Gulf states—or where enforcement is weak, and that contradicts the trade strategy rhetoric.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: We’re also worried about tariff-free quotas that may flood markets with cheap imports and harm good UK jobs in steel and manufacturing.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: Finally, ISDS threatens the Government's ability to act in the public interest; we want the UK to exclude ISDS from future deals, as Australia has done.

turns.speaker: Lord McDonald of Salford
turns.text: Thanks—Amrita, on development and environment, what’s your view?

turns.speaker: Amrita Saha
turns.text: On development, the UK’s Trade Advocacy Fund has helped poorer countries negotiate more effectively by paying for technical support, which is good value for money.

turns.speaker: Amrita Saha
turns.text: The DCTS tariff preferences are encouraging greater use by developing exporters and can help growth, but preferences alone don’t build domestic productive capacity.

turns.speaker: Amrita Saha
turns.text: We’ve seen some gender- and inclusion-focused measures, but programmes often lack coherence and funded implementation—especially with current aid cuts.

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: The trade strategy recognises trade’s social and environmental consequences, which we welcomed, but in many new deals those chapters aren’t enforceable—so they’re mostly rhetoric.

chapters.title: The WTO, reform and developing‑country capacity
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses want WTO reform that embeds labour standards, gives development flexibilities, and funds country-level negotiating capacity.

turns.speaker: Lord Anderson of Swansea
turns.text: Has the international climate for labour, environment and development worsened recently?

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: There are big problems at the WTO—blocked appellate body, and powerful members resisting change. But global unions still want a WTO that enforces fair trade, including labour rights.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: We argue labour standards should be embedded in WTO rules and that developing countries need flexibilities on subsidies, technology transfer and IP to build jobs.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Is enough being done to help countries build skills and processing capability at home?

turns.speaker: Amrita Saha
turns.text: Not consistently. Market access (like DCTS) is helpful, but countries need investments and targeted support to use those preferences—things like standards help, finance and infrastructure.

turns.speaker: Amrita Saha
turns.text: UK programmes that fund negotiation help are valuable; we recommend keeping and better targeting that support to country-level capacity too.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: Are the environmental terms the EU got with Mercosur the sort of thing the UK should seek?

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: I can’t assess the EU text point by point, but I would stress strategic priorities: investing negotiating capital wisely. Years-long FTAs often yield limited economic gains compared with other possible actions.

chapters.title: Types of agreements and the democratic gap
chapters.takeaway: The UK is using many non‑traditional deals and MoUs that escape parliamentary scrutiny; witnesses warn that reduces democratic accountability.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: Does the form of agreement—FTAs vs MoUs—matter and has the Government struck the right balance?

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: Yes it matters. The UK is doing many non-binding deals—critical minerals pacts, sectoral agreements—and those have had almost no parliamentary scrutiny, which is a democratic problem.

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: A notable example is the UK‑US pharma deal: academic analysis (which the witness cited) suggests it could raise NHS drug costs and, by one estimate, could be linked to large health impacts; yet it had no parliamentary debate.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: We share the scrutiny concern. Non-binding arrangements create uncertainty for workers and employers. Where legal commitments are needed—on labour or environment—we want them binding and clear.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: Have unions been able to influence non-binding deals?

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: We’re engaged—the TUC sits on the Trade and Labour Forum and domestic advisory groups—but access hasn’t always translated into binding clauses in some recent non‑EU deals.

chapters.title: ISDS, investor protections and public policy
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses argue ISDS overprotects foreign investors, carries little measurable investment benefit, and risks blocking public-interest policies.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury
turns.text: Do trade rules preserve governments’ ability to regulate in the public interest?

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: Not reliably. ISDS has been used to challenge public policies. The evidence that ISDS boosts foreign investment is very weak—one major review found its effect essentially zero.

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: The UK now faces three ISDS threats: a proposed coal mine in Cumbria seeking ~£300m; a claim by Russian investor Mikhail Fridman over sanctions; and a Chinese steel firm's challenge linked to Scunthorpe.

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: These cases show how ISDS can chill public policy—countries have started removing ISDS from new deals, and the UK should consider doing likewise.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is ISDS different from normal compensation for expropriation or contract breaches?

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: Yes: ISDS gives investors a private international tribunal route and very broad protections (fair and equitable treatment), which tribunals have interpreted expansively—beyond classic expropriation.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: We see ISDS as a privileged route unavailable to most others; it has been used against wage increases, public ownership and environmental policy—so it constrains democratic choices.

chapters.title: Practical support for development and local partnerships
chapters.takeaway: To make trade beneficial for developing countries, the UK should fund productive capacity building, support local actors, and pursue targeted co‑operation.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Could the UK use sectoral development compacts to tackle real barriers—power, finance, standards—so farmers and manufacturers in Africa benefit from preferences?

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: Yes. Trade policy should protect policy space for industrial policy and be combined with targeted support—trade rules plus finance, infrastructure and standards help are complementary.

turns.speaker: Amrita Saha
turns.text: We recommend continuing the Trade Advocacy Fund and directing more implementation funding to country-level programmes, linking trade preferences with investments in productive capacity.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: We’d also like the UK to fund trade-union capacity building in developing countries so workers' voices shape agreements—this used to be funded and made a measurable difference.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Do municipal-level partnerships help?

turns.speaker: Tom Wills
turns.text: Yes—local collaborations linking chambers of commerce, unions and local government can make trade more inclusive if they focus on supply chains and standards support.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: We have examples: northern England mayors met Indian unions and employers to promote sustainable investment and jobs; these local links are practical and promising.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final point: please send any follow-up evidence in writing—especially on figures like union membership in export sectors and on CPTPP details.

turns.speaker: Rosa Crawford
turns.text: I will write with membership figures and further material on CPTPP and the union perspective.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all—this has been a useful discussion for our inquiry into how the UK should deploy its trade instruments.
